Staub.et:
From Middle High German stoup, stoub from Old High German stoub, from Proto-West Germanic *staub, from Proto-Germanic *staubaz, related to *steubaną (“to smoke, fume, fly about”) (compare also Gestüpp). Related to stieben.
Cognate with Danish støv, Norwegian B…

s: congestion, stagnancy of water or anything dammed or otherwise backed-up
Stau.et: First attested in the 18th century, from Low German Stau, from Middle Low German stouw, stouwe (“weir”), probably a back-formation from stouwen (“to stop, dam”), from Old Saxon *stōwa, from Proto-West Germanic *stōu, ultimately derived from Proto-Germanic *stō…

s: to dam (block a river or similar by building a dam)
to accumulate, to build up, to get backed up
Wegen der Baustelle ist eine Spur gesperrt, deshalb staut sich hier der Verkehr.
Because of roadworks, one lane is blocked, so traffic is getting backed up here.
In Städten staut sich die Hitze oft besonders.
Heat often builds up in cities in particular.
stauen.et: From Middle High German stouwen, from Old High German stouwen, from Proto-West Germanic *stōjan.

Staubsauger.et:
From Staub (“dust”) + saugen (“to suck”) + -er.
The word itself is attested since at least 1846, originally in the textile industry. (see quote)

s: to be amazed or astonished; to wonder or marvel
Die Zuschauer staunten über seine Kunststücke.
The spectators were amazed at his tricks and feats.
Ich staune, dass das so gut funktioniert.
I'm astonished that that works so well.
staunen.et: Attested since the 17th century, then introduced in the general written language by Albrecht von Haller (1708-1777), from Alemannic German stūnen, of uncertain origin. Probably related to stauen (“to dam, retain”). Alternatively—though less likely both on sema…

s: to vacuum (to use a vacuum cleaner)
dustcloth, dustrag, duster (object used for dusting)

stauben.et: From Middle High German stouben, from Old High German stouben, from Proto-West Germanic *staubijan (“to sprinkle”). Equivalent to Staub + -en. Cognate with Hunsrik staave.

Staude.et: From Middle High German stūde, from Old High German stūda, probably related to stauen.

s: a cylindrical or slightly conical drinking vessel without a stem, typically with no handle, beaker
Stauf.et: From Middle High German stouf, from Old High German stouf, from Proto-Germanic, existing as a drinking vessel name as well in Middle Low German stōp, Old English stēap, English stoup, Old Norse staup.

s: to upset; to perform a forming operation that increases a workpiece's diameter by decreasing its length.
stauchen.et: Uncertain. Perhaps from Middle High German stūchen (“to cup, bleed”), from Middle High German stūche (“cupping glass”). Alternatively, perhaps from Middle Low German stûken (“to push, compress, arrange flax in small bundles for drying”), from Middle Low German…

s: to dust (cover with fine powder or liquid)
stäuben.et: From Middle High German stöuben, causative of stieben. Nowadays interpreted as Staub + -en.

s: a post to which an offender is tied in order to be flogged publicly
the act of publicly flogging someone at such a post
Staupe.et: 13th century, from northern Middle High German stūpe, from Middle Low German stûp, staup, from Polabian staup, from Proto-Slavic *stъlbъ (“post, pillar”).

Staumauer.et: From Stau (“blocked or dammed mass of water”) + Mauer (“wall”).

s: to tie (someone) to a post and flog them publicly
stäupen.et: 16th century, from Staupe (“post for public flagellation”), from Middle Low German staup, stûp, from Polabian staup, from Proto-Slavic *stъlbъ (“post, pillar”).

s: ramjet, athodyd (aero thermodynamic duct) (a form of airbreathing jet engine that uses the forward motion of the engine to produce thrust)
handsome fungus beetle (beetle in the family Endomychidae)
dust catcher; something that is rarely used and catches dust
